critiques.issue: There are no Lvl1 claims at all, so the loop has no structure to falsify. Any experiments run now will be untargeted parameter tweaks, and later 'improved' rows can't be credited to a mechanism.
critiques.suggestion: Before running any experiments, register 2–4 competing Lvl1 claims about what drives `time` at fixed accuracy ≥0.753. For example: H1, epochs-to-75% (sample efficiency) dominates; H2, per-epoch throughput (data pipeline, precision, compile, channels_last) dominates; H3, the CPU/data side (4 pinned cores, CPU augmentation, prepare-time loading) is the bottleneck; H4, seed variance sets how close to the accuracy threshold a recipe can safely be cut. Each one needs a Lvl3 prediction that a single run could refute.

critiques.issue: There is no baseline. Without the template recipe's accuracy and time, no later result can be called a speedup or a regression, and the 'improved' column means nothing.
critiques.suggestion: Run E001 as the unmodified submission_template on the 3 seeds. Record accuracy, time, and per-trial values, plus the prepare/train time split if the harness exposes it. This tells you whether H3 (prepare/data) or the train loop is the larger share.

critiques.target: noise floor (applies to all future conclusions)
critiques.issue: Each run gives a 3-seed mean, but the official judgment uses 40 seeds. Seed-to-seed accuracy SD on CIFAR-100 short schedules is often about 0.2–0.4 pp. The 3-seed mean's standard error is then about 0.15–0.25 pp, about the same as the 0.3 pp safety margin. Timing also varies from run to run (compile caches, GPU clocks, CPU contention). Right now no difference can be judged as larger or smaller than noise.
critiques.suggestion: Early on, rerun the baseline, or the first feasible recipe, 2–3 times to measure the SD of both accuracy and time. Make it a standing rule that any accuracy delta under about 2× the SE, or any time delta under the measured time jitter, is logged as ~ (inconclusive), not +/−. Do not mark a recipe as final if its accuracy is at 0.753–0.756 based on a single run.

critiques.target: rule-compliance risks (not yet a hypothesis, but they will invalidate results)
critiques.issue: Several easy wins are illegal or fragile. (1) Warming up or compiling in `build` with real data is forbidden; only synthetic inputs are allowed. (2) `prepare` must reset EMA, optimizer, scheduler and RNG state, and it is easy to leak state through a compiled module or cached tensors between trials. (3) Eval must return [B,100] logits for any B from 1 to 1024 within 5 s. A torch.compile'd model with static shapes can recompile for every new B and blow that budget. (4) Test-time augmentation such as flip-averaging is banned, even though airbench-style recipes use it.
critiques.suggestion: Add a compliance check to every candidate. Use dynamic=True, or an uncompiled or padded eval path, for arbitrary B. Explicitly re-init everything in prepare. Do not carry over flip TTA from CIFAR-10 speedrun recipes; plan for losing roughly 0.3–0.5 pp from it.

critiques.target: never-tried directions (prior art to seed Lvl2s)
critiques.issue: Without hypotheses, the obvious known-strong directions aren't registered: GPU-resident data with on-GPU random crop and flip (this matters on 4 CPU cores); bf16/channels_last with torch.compile done in build; airbench/hlb-style small ResNet or VGG-ish nets with BatchNorm and whitening init; label smoothing; one-cycle/linear-decay LR with large batch; Lookahead or EMA; progressive resizing; and the trade-off between batch size and step count.
critiques.suggestion: Turn these into Lvl2 mechanisms under H1 and H2 with quantitative Lvl3 predictions. Example: 'moving augmentation to GPU cuts time by ≥X% at unchanged accuracy (±0.2 pp)'. Prioritize the ones that change time without touching accuracy, because those are cheapest to confirm under 3-seed noise.

critiques.issue: Local runs use an A100 SXM4. Judging uses an A100 PCIe, which has a lower TDP and clocks and different sustained throughput. A recipe tuned to the edge of compute or memory bandwidth may rank differently on PCIe, and absolute times will not transfer.
critiques.suggestion: Treat absolute `time` as local only. Prefer changes that reduce total work (fewer epochs or FLOPs) over micro-tuning for SXM throughput, and record this caveat in any Lvl3 prediction about kernel-level gains.

critiques.issue: The objective is lexicographic: maximize accuracy until 0.753, then minimize time. The loop may optimize time on recipes that aren't yet feasible, or overshoot accuracy by a large margin, which wastes time.
critiques.suggestion: Find a feasible recipe with some margin (about 0.76) first. Then cut epochs or width along a measured accuracy-vs-time curve, with at least 3 points, to find the cheapest setting that clears 0.753 with noise-aware margin. Don't do one-off cuts.

structured_output.summary: The hypothesis tree, results, predictions and notebook are all empty, so there are no conclusions or contradictions to review and nothing yet to rest on a single run or on noise. The main risk is structural. Experiments started without competing Lvl1 claims, a baseline or a noise estimate will produce changes that can't be credited to any mechanism. Next steps: register Lvl1 claims (sample efficiency, per-epoch throughput, CPU/data bottleneck, seed-variance margin). Run the template baseline, then rerun it to measure accuracy and time SD, because the 0.3 pp safety margin is about the size of the 3-seed standard error. Build compliance checks into every candidate: no real data in build, full reset in prepare, eval that works for any B within 5 s, and no TTA. Finally, keep in mind that times measured on the local SXM GPU won't carry over directly to the PCIe judging GPU.
